title: Coming back well
hook: a forest monk who returns to the community should come back with respect

segments.voice: Yesterday: why he speaks of rebirth. Not to boast, but so the living can be inspired. Your line was to inspire. Whose small, true goodness did you pass on? Day four hundred sixty-one.

You've been away. Six months working remotely, a semester abroad, a long stretch of caring for a parent in another city. Now you're walking back into the office, the class, the family dinner. Everyone has moved on a bit. There are new jokes you don't get. And there's a temptation, quietly, to come back as the one who's been somewhere. A monk named Gulissāni lived in the forest, alone. One day he comes into the monastery on some business. And Sāriputta takes the opportunity to give a talk about how to come back.
screen: `YOU'VE BEEN AWAY.` → `NEW JOKES YOU DON'T GET.` → `GULISSĀNI COMES IN FROM THE FOREST.`

segments.voice: Sāriputta doesn't scold Gulissāni. He speaks to the room. A forest monk who comes back to the community, he says, should be respectful and deferential toward his companions. If he isn't, people will say: what good is all his solitude, if he can't even treat his fellow monks with respect? Then come the details, and they're wonderfully ordinary. Be skilled about where you sit. Don't push in on the elders, and don't push the younger monks off their seats. Don't go into the village too early, or come back too late. Don't drop in on families before or after the meal. Don't be restless or fidgety. Don't chatter. Be easy to correct. Guard your senses, eat in moderation, stay awake and mindful. And knowing the teaching matters too: people will ask the forest monk about it. Every item ends the same way. If he doesn't do this, there'll be some who say: what's the use of his forest life? Then Moggallāna asks a good question. Is this only for forest monks? No, says Sāriputta. It's even more so for those who live near a village. The point isn't that solitude is suspect; nothing in the sutta speaks against the forest. The point is that solitude is tested in company. Whatever you gained alone shows up in where you sit, when you arrive, and how well you take correction. Coming back well isn't a performance of humility. It's where the time away shows.
screen: `SPEAKING TO THE ROOM.` · `WHERE YOU SIT, WHEN YOU ARRIVE.` · `EASY TO CORRECT.` · `VILLAGE MONKS TOO.` · then, large: `COME BACK WELL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rejoin one group well. Sit and settle. Think of a group you'll walk back into soon, a team, a class, a family table, a friend circle you've drifted from. Picture arriving. Where will you sit? Who might you listen to first, instead of telling your news? Who's younger, or newer, that you could make room for? Let the picture be small and practical. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Coming back well. Sāriputta's advice to a forest monk returning to the community: respect, good timing, easy to correct. Solitude tested in company. Today's word.
Your line: come back well. Today, when you rejoin any group, arrive on time, listen first, and make room for someone newer. Day four hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: In Theravada forest lineages, monks may spend stretches in solitude and then return to the monastery for communal occasions, where seating follows seniority and courtesy to fellow monastics is expected.

original.note: Pali gārava: respect, reverence. the first thing Sāriputta asks of a returning forest monk.

trapdoor: what you thought: coming back means just showing up again.
what it means: returning with respect, good timing and openness to correction, so the time away shows in how you treat others.
what a scholar hears: MN 69, the Gulissāni Sutta, given by Sāriputta, not the Buddha; it lists qualities from courtesy and moderation up to knowledge of the teaching and the training.

notes: MN 69 paraphrased; the list of qualities is condensed and partly reordered; confirm.
The sutta's higher items (Abhidhamma and Abhivinaya, peaceful liberations, superhuman states) are summarized as 'knowing the teaching'; confirm this is fair.
gārava as the key term for 'respectful' (sagārava) should be confirmed.
